title: Tour Pooling vs Consolidation vs Wholesale
excerpt: Tour pooling, consolidation and wholesale compared for Egyptian operators: who sells to the traveller, who sets the price, and which model fits.
body_html:
Prices, timetables and visiting details are a November 2026 snapshot. Check the linked official pages and your departure’s current inclusions and terms before booking.

Quick answer

The three models differ in who stands between you and the traveller, and who sets the price. In pooling, several agencies fill one confirmed departure: the operating agency runs it under its own licence and is named, and the platform sets the price and brings the seats. In consolidation, a consolidator gathers your scheduled seats and resells them under its own brand. In wholesale, you give net rates to DMCs and wholesalers, who mark them up and sell on, so your margin ceiling is the net rate. Choose by what you can least afford to lose: the guest relationship, the margin, or the date.

The Egyptian Travel Agents Association provides an independent place to check agency membership.

Key facts

Fact Detail
Pooling Several agencies fill one date of a fixed tour. On Sawa the date confirms at four travellers, with eight at most
Consolidation A consolidator aggregates seat inventory from many operators and resells it through its own channels
Wholesale You publish net rates to DMCs and wholesalers, who add their mark-up and sell through their own networks
Who sets the price Pooling on Sawa: Sawa, from its rate card. Consolidation: usually the consolidator. Wholesale: you set the net rate; the wholesaler sets the selling price
How you earn on Sawa The operating agency: operating costs plus an agreed fee, plus the pool share on seats it sold itself. A selling agency: a share of the pool for each seat sold, paid as set in the agency agreement. Sawa takes 10% of the selling price and there is no fee to join
Risk of a thin date Pooling: a date that does not reach four is cancelled, nothing is charged, and another date is suggested. Consolidation and wholesale: set by the contract
Best used As a mix. The models are channels, not identities

Every Egyptian operator knows the Friday problem: the guide is booked, the vehicle is booked, the permits are paid, and half the seats are empty. Fixed costs do not care whether two travellers ride or eight. There are three established ways to close that gap: pool your departures with other agencies, sell your seats through a consolidator, or contract net rates to DMCs. They differ sharply on brand, margin and control. This guide compares them, operator to operator. It comes from the team behind Sawa Tours (sawa.tours), where the founder has worked in Egyptian tourism since 1993. We run a pooling platform, so read the comparison with that in mind: the facts first, the pitch last.

The problem: seats you cannot sell alone

Seat-in-coach touring has an awkward cost shape. The guide, the vehicle and much of the day's cost are the same whether two travellers show up or eight. Below the break-even number, every date is a choice between two losses: cancel and bear the refunds and the reputational damage, or run it and absorb the loss. The arithmetic is in our guide to break-even group size, and the cost of cancelling is in why operators cancel under-filled departures.

The demand to fill those seats often exists but is fragmented. Several agencies each hold two or three travellers for the same Abu Simbel Thursday, all below their minimums, all facing the same cancellation. The three models below are three answers to that fragmentation.

The three models, defined

Tour pooling

Pooling puts other agencies' travellers on a departure alongside your own. When the combined count clears the minimum, the date confirms and runs, with an operating agency's guide, vehicle and itinerary. A pooling platform handles the parts agencies cannot do alone: finding and matching travellers, confirming the date and collecting payments.

On Sawa, travellers from several licensed agencies and direct bookers reserve seats on one date of a fixed tour. A date confirms, the GoAhead, when four travellers have reserved it, and a group is never larger than eight. As an illustration: two of your travellers, three from another agency and two booked directly make seven on a date that none of you could have confirmed alone. Agencies can also sell through Sawa's booking widget on their own websites, with bookings credited to their referral code.

Consolidation

A consolidator aggregates scheduled-seat inventory from many operators and resells it through its own brand and channels. You become a supplier: you deliver the operation while the consolidator owns the storefront and the booking. Consolidation buys reach you may not have, such as search visibility, foreign demand and agent networks, at the price of invisibility: the traveller tends to remember the platform, not you. You are also one supplier among many on the same shelf, so price pressure is a risk.

Wholesale and DMC contracts

Wholesale is the classic contract route. You publish net rates to DMCs and wholesalers, who add their mark-up and sell packages through their own networks. Done well it is dependable volume with predictable operations: you deal with one partner rather than dozens of travellers. The trade is structural. The net rate is your margin ceiling by definition, the DMC deals with the guest, and your capacity is committed to partners whose demand can swing with exchange rates and seasons.

The comparison: who stands between you and the traveller, margin and risk

Pooling (on Sawa) Consolidation Wholesale / DMC
Who sells to the traveller Sawa and the selling agencies The consolidator The DMC or wholesaler
Your name The operating agency is named to travellers before the deposit is due Usually not visible to the traveller Usually not visible to the traveller
Who sets the price Sawa, from its rate card Usually the consolidator You set the net rate; the wholesaler sets the selling price
Your return Operating agency: costs plus an agreed fee, plus the pool share on its own seats. Selling agency: a share of the pool, paid as set in the agency agreement Your supply price, per the contract Your net rate
Payment Online Era collects payments by secure payment link, as agent for the operating agency; nothing is charged before the GoAhead Per the consolidator's terms Per the contract
Volume certainty Per date: a date confirms at four, or is cancelled with nothing charged Aggregated demand, but you are replaceable Highest where contracted, but seasonal
Control over the day The operating agency runs the guide, vehicle and itinerary You operate to their specification You operate to the contract specification
Best for Agencies with strong operations and thin demand Agencies with surplus seats and no brand abroad Agencies with coach-scale capacity and contracts

Read the table twice, once for margin and once for control. On margin, wholesale may bring volume and pooling a share of a fixed price. On control, pooling is the model where the operating agency still runs the departure, the guide and the vehicle, while someone else solves demand.

Which model suits which operator

Three questions sort it.

  • Brand. If repeat business and word of mouth are your growth engine, anything that hides your name costs more than it pays. Consolidation and wholesale hide it; pooling names the operating agency.
  • Margin floor. If your pricing already runs thin, a net rate below your usual selling price is not a model, it is a discount. Work out your contribution per traveller before you sign anything.
  • Capacity. If you own coach-scale capacity and can staff a contracted calendar, wholesale deserves the meeting. If your fleet is a van or two, it probably does not.

The honest answer for most Egyptian operators is a mix: contracts for the base load you can bank, pooling for the dates your own channels leave short, and consolidation sparingly. The models are channels, not identities. The mistake is running one by default instead of by decision.

Where Sawa fits: pooling, built for Egyptian operators

Sawa (sawa.tours) is a pooling marketplace operated by Online Era (registration 148500). It runs a fixed catalogue with its own calendar and prices. There is no fee to join, and Sawa takes 10% of the selling price. Calculations are in Egyptian pounds and agencies are paid in euros.

An agency can take two roles. As a selling agency it sells seats and earns a share of the pool for each seat, paid as set in the agency agreement. Each departure is operated by one of the licensed agencies with travellers on the date, named before the deposit is due; that operating agency runs the day under its own licence and is entitled to its operating costs plus an agreed fee, and it also earns the pool share on the seats it sold itself. To join, an agency needs a Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities licence, ETAA registration and insurance. Newer agencies are welcome but must show references or a portfolio; we check the documents and confirm the licence with the Ministry (verify).

Travellers reserve free and pay nothing until the date confirms. At four travellers the date reaches the GoAhead. On a day tour a 10% deposit is due then and the balance 2 days (48 hours) before departure, and a forming date has until 7 days before the tour to reach four; on packages and cruises the deposit is 25%, the balance is due 14 days before, and a date must reach four by 30 days before. A date that misses four is cancelled with nothing charged, and another date is suggested. Travellers can also start their own date, which Sawa reviews. See how to apply for the process.

The short version

Three models, one ledger: pool to fill thin dates while the operating agency still runs the tour, consolidate for reach you cannot build, and use wholesale for volume you can bank. Price each by what you give up. If fixed costs are eating your thin dates, pooling is the model where someone else brings the seats and you still run the departure. Apply at sawa.tours/operators: there is no fee to join, and you choose by what you cannot afford to lose, the guest relationship, the margin or the date.
